凱爾特豎琴又稱愛爾蘭豎琴，屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號322: The Celtic harp, also called the Irish harp, is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.221. It has a triangular frame and a soundbox, no pedals and no tuning mechanism, and different strings give different notes; it has no semitones, and the sound is a sustained one; the player plucks the strings with the fingernails. It was traditionally current in the Celtic regions of Ireland, Scotland, Wales and Brittany, was used on aristocratic occasions in Ireland and Scotland, and in Wales was played by professional musicians.

At early Irish aristocratic banquets the poets and cruit players were seated with the nobility; the Gaelic nobility of Ireland and Scotland also used the instrument for a long time. The records show that the Irish ensemble combined the harp with the tympanum, and that Scotland added the crowd as well. In Wales it was played by professional musicians, the clerwyr. 歐洲西北部凱爾特三角框豎琴的早期歷史有爭議。蓋爾世界最早與豎琴傳統相關的樂器稱: The early history of the triangular Celtic harp of north-west Europe is disputed. The earliest instrument in the Gaelic world connected with the harp tradition was called the cruit, a word perhaps related to the Welsh crwth; clàrsach / cláirseach may be of Scottish origin. A triangular harp with horsehair strings already appears in 8th-century Pictish carvings, and it later reached Anglo-Saxon England and Ireland. The metal-strung harps of Ireland and Scotland were once associated with the nobility, and brass strings are common in the 1500s; more than 220 pieces by Turlough O'Carolan survive from the 17th and 18th centuries. At the end of the 18th century the craft declined, in the early 19th century a new gut-strung harp appeared in Ireland, and the Scottish Gaelic revival of the 1890s produced a similar new harp; today the strings are mostly nylon.
